The miracles are legend. The prophecies were back-dated. The Book, dissected and conjectured and reconstructed, turns out to be noble ancient literature — inspiring, of course, but hardly a voice you must obey.

Notice the move, because Satan has run it since the garden. He doesn't have to burn the Book anymore. He only has to get you looking at the man in front of it — the scholar, the professor, the expert — *instead of searching the Scriptures for yourself.* Control the guides, and you quietly control the crowd. So the most Bible-saturated civilization in history talked itself out of its own Bible without a single chain. A Book that is doubted never has to be banned. It just lies there, open and unread, robbed of its power to correct anyone — while the same two Eden lies stroll in through the front door: *you shall not surely die,* and *you get to decide for yourself what is true.*

That is the world the last deception found already furnished and waiting for it.

notes.beat: Spirit-contact returns dressed for the modern West — meditation, mysticism, channeling: the religion of Babel again, 'ye shall not surely die' in a wellness studio.
notes.oldNote: Now look at our own century — the one that laughed the old gods off the stage. The same spirit-contact came back dressed for the modern West: meditation that empties the mind and invites what fills it, mysticism that seeks the god within, channeling, spirit guides, energy work. Strip away the vocabulary and it is the religion of Babel again: the soul is divine, the soul cannot die, and the spirits will speak if you open the door. The serpent’s sermon in a wellness studio: ye shall not surely die.
notes.newNote:
Now bring the story into our own century — the age that laughed the old gods off the stage and called witchcraft a fable of the Dark Ages. But the thing itself never left. It only changed its clothes. The same spirit-contact came back dressed for the modern West: meditation that empties the mind and invites whatever fills it, mysticism that hunts the god within, channeling, spirit guides, energy work. And notice where it walked in — not the fringe. It moved into the science labs, into the churches, into the halls where laws are made. The name "witchcraft" we hold in contempt; the thing we welcomed, because it flatters us.

Strip away the soft vocabulary and it is the religion of Babel wearing new robes: the soul is divine, the soul cannot die, and the spirits will speak the moment you open the door. And listen to what the voice always says — no matter who you are, no matter what you believe, live as you please; heaven is your home. That is not new. That is the oldest sermon on earth, first preached under a tree in a garden. The serpent's whisper, now in a wellness studio: ye shall not surely die.

notes.beat: The oldest mask returns — mediums and grief 'visitations' aim straight at love; but the dead sleep, and your beloved dead are safe beyond every impostor.
notes.oldNote: And the oldest mask of all is back. Mediums fill theaters. Grief ‘visitations’ feel utterly real. The departed seem to send signs, to speak, to visit dreams. It is the cruelest point of attack, because it aims straight at love. But the Book has not moved: the dead sleep (Ecclesiastes 9:5; John 11:11-14) — and whatever stands there wearing a beloved face studied that face for a lifetime. And land this as mercy, not horror: your beloved dead are safe — asleep, beyond the reach of every impostor. Hold on to what hangs on this — everything the deceiver has left rides on it.
notes.newNote:
And now the oldest mask of all comes back — the very first lie, wearing a new face. Mediums fill theaters. Grief "visitations" feel utterly real: the departed seem to send a sign, to speak a word, to slip into a dream. And this is the cruelest place the enemy could aim, because he aims straight at love — at the ache of the one you'd give anything to hold again.

But the Book hasn't moved. The dead sleep — they know nothing, they wait (Ecclesiastes 9:5; John 11:11-14, where Jesus Himself calls death "sleep"). So whatever stands there wearing a beloved face is not your beloved. It is an impostor that studied that face for a lifetime.

Now land this as mercy, not horror. Your beloved dead are safe — asleep, quiet, utterly beyond the reach of every counterfeit that would trade on their memory. Nothing can touch them there. Hold on to that, because everything the deceiver has left rides on getting you to let it go.

notes.beat: For unbelievers the mask changes costume — UFOs and channeled star-voices preaching the same doctrines; masks rotate, the script never changes.
notes.oldNote: And for a generation that believes in neither gods nor ghosts? The masquerade changes costume once more. Lights over the cities, visitors from other worlds, channeled voices from the stars — entities that somehow always preach the same old doctrines: humanity is divine, death is not real, no Saviour required. Ancestor, deity, alien — the masks rotate; the actors and the script never change. And Jesus said the wonders would escalate as the end approaches: ‘insomuch that, if it were possible, they shall deceive the very elect’ (Matthew 24:24).
notes.newNote:
And for a generation that believes in neither gods nor ghosts — what then? The masquerade simply changes costume one last time. Now it's lights hanging over the cities, visitors said to come from other worlds, voices channeled down from the stars. And listen to what these "advanced beings" always seem to teach: humanity is secretly divine, death isn't real, no Saviour required. Notice it's the very same message — the oldest lie in the world, dressed for a skeptical age.

Ancestor, deity, alien: the masks keep rotating, but the actor behind them never changes, and neither does his script. And Jesus told us the wonders would only grow more dazzling as the end draws near — "insomuch that, if it were possible, they shall deceive the very elect" (Matthew 24:24).

notes.beat: The masquerade peaks: Satan himself as an angel of light with lying wonders and the dead appearing to preach — both Eden lies at once; contrast the true Christ who comes with clouds.
notes.oldNote: And before He comes, the masquerade reaches its peak: Satan himself as an angel of light, with all power and signs and lying wonders. Wonders in place of the Word — and the crowning wonder: the dead appearing to speak and preach. Both Eden lies at once. Because if the dead are alive, the serpent was right. Mark the difference from what you saw a moment ago — the true Christ comes with clouds and every eye sees Him at once (Revelation 1:7); this one descends to a hillside crowd, working wonders instead of speaking the Word.
notes.newNote:
And before He comes, the masquerade reaches its peak. Story of Redemption traces every thread of it back to one garden. In Eden the serpent told Eve two lies in a single breath: "Ye shall not surely die," and "ye shall be as gods." Now, at the end, Satan cashes them both in at once.

First he works with real power — not tricks, but signs and lying wonders, fire called down in the sight of men. Wonders in the place of the Word. And the crowning wonder: the dead appearing to speak. Beloved faces you buried come back to preach — and every one of them, Ellen White says, denies the Book and tells you heaven is home no matter how you live. Because if the dead are alive, the serpent was right about death. And if they can lead you back to God on their own terms, the serpent was right about being as gods. Both Eden lies, walking and talking.

Then the masterpiece: Satan himself, an angel of light, a majestic being of dazzling brightness — a glory beyond anything mortal eyes have seen. The crowd falls down; the cry goes up, "Christ has come!" His voice is soft and full of melody; he heals their diseases and speaks gentle, gracious words. It is almost overmastering.

But mark the difference from what you saw a moment ago. This one descends to a hillside crowd and works wonders instead of speaking the Word. The true Christ comes with clouds, and every eye — the whole world at once — sees Him (Revelation 1:7). That coming cannot be counterfeited. So when someone says, "He is here, He is in the secret chamber," don't go. The real Lord will not need an introduction.

notes.beat: The strategy's endgame: a counterfeit unity crying peace and safety — every path one mountain — on the eve of sudden destruction.
notes.oldNote: And what is all this masquerade FOR? Watch the strategy: distraction, then war, then the great cry — peace and safety. Out of fear and chaos, a counterfeit unity: every religion one family, every path one mountain, all roads leading home. It will sound like heaven has come to earth. Paul says it is the eve of sudden destruction.
notes.newNote:
And what is all this masquerade FOR? Here's the endgame. Watch the strategy run its course: distraction, then war, then — out of the fear and the smoke — a great cry goes up. Peace and safety. Peace at last.

And listen to how it will sound. Not like a threat. Like heaven itself has finally come down. Every religion, one family. Every path, one mountain. All roads leading home. The great deceiver has spent the whole war engineering this moment: powers that never belonged together reaching across the old chasms to clasp hands — church and state and the spirit-world, all folding into one glowing embrace. It will be the most beautiful thing the world has ever seen. Voices soft and full of melody. A blessing pronounced over the whole earth. Christ has come, they'll say — and the crowds will fall down and worship.

But it's a counterfeit. The unity is a costume over a chasm. And Paul saw it two thousand years ago: the very hour the whole world is crying "peace and safety" — that is the eve of sudden destruction, coming as a thief in the night, when no one thought to look up.

notes.beat: The old geography returns — 'come out of her, my people'; a people quietly separates from Babylon's last delicious golden age, distinction their protection.
notes.oldNote: And just before He comes, the old geography returns one final time. You have seen this picture before — the mountains and the plain. Heaven's last call is a call of distinction: 'Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues' (Revelation 18:4). And Babylon's epitaph reads like the plain of old: 'How much she hath glorified herself, and lived deliciously' (Revelation 18:7) — living deliciously, one last golden age in the doomed lowlands. So once again a people quietly separates: simpler lives, harder lives, further from the noise — not fleeing the world's people but its bewitching, keeping the lamps trimmed where the Word can still be heard. Two civilizations again; two seeds still. Distinction was their protection then. It is ours now — because what falls on the plain this time is not water.
notes.newNote:
And just before the end, the old geography returns one last time. You have seen this picture before — the mountains and the plain. Heaven's final call is a call of distinction, one clear voice cutting through everything: "Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues." A mighty angel comes down, the whole earth is lit with his glory, and the cry goes up — Babylon is fallen. And Babylon's epitaph reads like the plain of old: she "hath glorified herself, and lived deliciously" — one last golden age in the doomed lowlands, deaf to the warning, "lulled into a fatal security."

But the light reaches the honest ones wherever they are, and they answer. Ellen White saw them "hurried out of the doomed churches, as Lot was hurried out of Sodom before her destruction" — the call carried even to the poorest, even to slaves, who sang for joy at their deliverance while their masters stood silent, unable to stop them. So once again a people quietly separates — not fleeing the world's people but its bewitching, drawn out toward higher ground where the Word can still be heard. Two civilizations again; two seeds still. Distinction was their protection then. It is ours now — because what falls on the plain this time is not water.

notes.beat: Against the cry of many ways stands one sentence: I am the way, the truth, and the life — truth is a Person.
notes.oldNote: Against the cry of many ways stands one sentence: I am the way, the truth, and the life. Not A way — THE way. Truth is not a mood, and not a consensus. Truth is a person. And every other road is built on a world already under sentence.
notes.newNote:
Every age has a chorus telling people there are a thousand doors to God — build your own ladder, pick your own truth, follow your heart. Story of Redemption calls that the impending conflict: the last great struggle is not East against West, it's truth against a counterfeit. The enemy's whole strategy, Ellen White says, is simply this — divert the mind from Jesus. Set up a nicer idol. A philosophical god, a god of the poets and the polished universities, a god shaped to fit the age — and it turns out to be no better than Baal.

Against that whole chorus stands one sentence, spoken by a man to His friends the night before He died: I am the way, the truth, and the life. Notice — not A way. THE way. Truth here is not a mood you feel or a majority you count. Truth is a Person, standing in the room. He said it another way once: I am the door. Not one gate among many — the only door. Everyone who tries to climb into the fold some other way, He said plainly, is a thief and a robber. And the reason is stark: in Him is life — original, His own, underived. Every other road promises life it doesn't have to give, because it is built on a world already under sentence.

So the question tonight isn't "which of the many ways feels right to you." It's the older, quieter one: are your feet planted on the Rock — or on the sand the whole world is standing on?

notes.beat: Pivot from settled history to unturned pages — this world is almost over and One is coming with clouds; every eye shall see Him.
notes.oldNote: Everything so far is settled history — the cross is behind us. But the Book has pages not yet turned. It says this present world is almost over, and One is coming back: 'Behold, he cometh with clouds; and every eye shall see him' (Revelation 1:7). Pivot the room here: from what God HAS done to what He has PROMISED to do. Soon. And the nearer that day comes, the harder the old deceiver works — with the same two lies he drew in Eden.
notes.newNote:
Everything so far tonight is settled history. The cross is behind us; the tomb is empty; that page is written and cannot be unwritten. But the Book has pages not yet turned — and the last of them describe a morning still ahead of us.

Story of Redemption tells it like a scene you can almost stand inside. At the darkest hour, when the world has all but given up on any rescue, a small black cloud appears in the eastern sky, no bigger than a man's hand. It draws nearer, and it brightens — until it is a great white cloud ablaze at its base like fire, crowned with the rainbow of God's covenant. And upon it rides One the whole world will recognize. No crown of thorns now — a diadem of glory. His face outshining the noonday sun. "Behold, he cometh with clouds; and every eye shall see him" (Revelation 1:7).

Pivot the room right here: from what God HAS done — the cross — to what He has PROMISED to do. This present world is almost over, and One is coming back. Not a rumor, not a symbol — a face every eye will see.

And here is the tension to leave hanging: the nearer that day comes, the harder the old deceiver works. He is out of pages. So he reaches for the two lies he told at the very beginning, in a garden, to the first two people who ever lived.

notes.beat: The proud world-system is temporary and under sentence — the world passeth away, but he that doeth God's will abides forever.
notes.oldNote: The proud world-system — its money, its empires, its defiance — is temporary and already under sentence: 'the world passeth away' (1 John 2:17). Not cynicism, realism: what looks permanent is passing; what looks fragile — 'he that doeth the will of God' — abides for ever. (Revelation's own name for this world-system is 'Babylon' — Daniel's fallen empire reused as a symbol — and it announces her fall, Revelation 18:2. That is a study of its own: one more reason to open Revelation together.)
notes.newNote:
Look at it: money, empires, the swagger of defiance — it feels permanent, doesn't it? It always does. In the closing scenes of the story, the proud world-system is still triumphant, still mocking. Its ministers had told everyone, "Peace, peace — all will be well." Its powers had cornered God's faithful people and jeered, "Where is your God now? Why doesn't He save you?" Right up to the last midnight, the world looks like it's winning.

And then God speaks. One sentence, rolling through the earth like thunder — and in an instant the whole thing turns. The mockers fall silent, the triumph collapses, and the ones who looked fragile, the ones who simply did the will of God, are the ones left standing forever.

That's not cynicism about the world — it's realism. "The world passeth away," John wrote, "but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever" (1 John 2:17). What looks unshakable is already passing; what looks small will outlast it all.

(Revelation has a name for this proud system — "Babylon," Daniel's fallen empire reused as a symbol — and it announces her fall outright: "Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen" (Revelation 18:2). That's a whole study of its own. One more reason to open Revelation together.)

notes.beat: The old earth passes away in fire — not annihilation but a cleansing, the doorway the world passes through.
notes.oldNote: The old earth itself passes away in fire: 'the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt… the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up' (2 Peter 3:10). Not annihilation for its own sake — a cleansing, the doorway the world passes through. The destruction is real, and it is not the end of the story.
notes.newNote:
Hold this scene gently — it is the hardest image of the night, and Story of Redemption sets it inside the chapter it calls "The Second Death," right after Satan himself bows and confesses that his sentence is just. Only then does the fire come. So say it that way: this is not rage, it is the last honest verdict, agreed to by everyone — even the accuser.

Then let the picture roll. Fire comes down from God out of heaven; the earth breaks open, and the very rocks catch fire. "The heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt… the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up" (2 Peter 3:10). Ellen White pictures the whole surface of the world as one molten mass — a vast, seething lake of fire. It is total. Don't soften the destruction; it is real.

But here is the turn — and it's everything. While the earth is wrapped in that fire, the righteous abide safely in the Holy City; the second death has no power over them. And the fire that consumes also cleanses: "every trace of the curse is swept away." This is not annihilation for its own sake. It is the doorway the world passes through — the old, sin-scarred earth burned clean so a new one can rise in its place. Land the line: the destruction is real, but it is not the end of the story. The very next chapter is called "The New Earth."

notes.beat: A great final reckoning — the books opened, the dead judged by works — but framed as the same fair court whose Judge proved His fairness at the cross.
notes.oldNote: A great final reckoning — 'the books were opened… and the dead were judged… according to their works' (Revelation 20:11-12). Frame it inside the trial the night built: this is the SAME open court, the same just Judge whose fairness the universe watched Him prove at infinite cost — not a new threat. IF ASKED 'judged by works — but saved not by works?': no contradiction — the books establish the facts of the case; the book of LIFE holds those who accepted the rescue. Judged by works, saved by grace. Sober, not threatening — this is why the invitation matters.
notes.newNote:
A great final reckoning — the last court in all of history. "I saw a great white throne… and the books were opened… and the dead were judged according to their works" (Revelation 20:11-12). But before you picture a cold verdict, tell them what stands above the throne: the cross. In that hour the whole story is replayed for every eye like a panorama — Bethlehem, the years of mercy, the agony in the garden, the trial through the night streets, Calvary — the very trial this night has walked them through. This is not a new threat. It is the SAME open court, the same Judge whose fairness the universe already watched Him prove at infinite cost to Himself.

And here is the wonder: at the end, no one argues. Every lying excuse is swept away, and even the lost — seeing the cross for what it always was — join the saved in one verdict about God Himself: "Just and true are Thy ways." The court that condemns sin is the court that clears God's name, because the Judge paid the price He is asking about.

IF ASKED "judged by works — but saved not by works?": no contradiction. The books establish the facts of the case; the book of LIFE holds those who accepted the rescue. Judged by works, saved by grace.

So keep the tone sober, never threatening. This is exactly why the invitation matters — the fairest court in the universe has already opened its book of life, and the door is still open tonight.

notes.beat: The trial's final scene: history replayed above the throne, then unanimity — every knee bows, even the lost and the accuser concede God is just.
notes.oldNote: And then the trial this whole night has been tracing reaches its final scene. Above the great throne the entire history you have watched tonight is replayed — the whole panorama, from a cherub's first envy to the last deception — before every eye, with nothing hidden. And when it ends, something happens that has never happened in the history of the universe: unanimity. 'Every knee shall bow… and every tongue shall confess' (Philippians 2:10-11; Romans 14:11) — the saved in wonder, the lost in acknowledgment, and the accuser himself, out of arguments at last, bowing with them. No one is forced down; the evidence does it. Even the lost concede the verdict: God is just. The question Epicurus asked at the start of tonight gets its final answer in front of every being who ever lived — and not one voice dissents.
notes.newNote:
And so the trial this whole night has been tracing reaches its last scene. Above the great throne the cross appears — and against it the entire history you have watched tonight is replayed, like a panorama unrolling before every eye: a cherub's first envy, Eden, the long story of the plan to win us back, all the way down to that night of horror in Jerusalem and the last deception. Nothing is hidden, nothing softened. It appears, Scripture says, "just as it was."

And here is the thing that undoes every onlooker: no one can turn away. Each actor recalls the part he played. The redeemed see it and cast their crowns, crying, "He died for me!" But the lost see it too — and out of their own mouths comes the verdict. "All this," the lost soul cries, "I might have had." Every one of them concedes their exclusion is just. And the accuser himself, out of arguments at last, his charges against God's mercy silenced, bows down and confesses that the sentence is right.

Then something happens that has never happened in the history of the universe: unanimity. Every knee bows and every tongue confesses (Philippians 2:10-11) — the saved in wonder, the lost in acknowledgment, the accuser with them. No one is forced down; the evidence does it. The whole universe, loyal and rebellious alike, with one voice declares: "Just and true are Thy ways." The question Epicurus asked at the start of tonight gets its final answer in front of every being who ever lived — and not one voice dissents.

notes.beat: Revelation 21:4 — no more death, sorrow, or pain; a restored earth, the home you were made for, is what the fire made room for.
notes.oldNote: Revelation 21:4 — no more death, sorrow, crying, or pain. Not clouds and harps — a restored earth, the home you were made for. The groaning of the world, ended personally. After the fire: 'I saw a new heaven and a new earth' (Revelation 21:1). THIS is what the destruction was making room for.
notes.newNote:
Watch what the fire actually does. In John's vision it isn't the end of the story — it's the turning of the page. The same flame that ends evil doesn't leave a scorched ruin behind; it *purifies*. Every trace of the curse — every thorn, every grave, every scar the long war left on this planet — swept clean away. And what rises out of it is not a place of clouds and harps in some far-off sky. It's *ground*. A country. A home. The kingdom this world forfeited so long ago, handed back.

"I saw a new heaven and a new earth" (Revelation 21:1) — and then the promise everyone in this room has ached for without knowing its name: God "shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away" (Revelation 21:4). The groaning of the whole world — and the private grief you carry into this tent tonight — ended. Personally. By His own hand.

There is one scar left in the universe. Not on the earth. On Him — the marks in His hands and feet, the only reminder that any of this ever happened. THIS is the home you were made for. THIS is what the fire was making room for.

notes.beat: Affliction shall not rise a second time — peace secured not by force but by a verdict the whole universe witnessed; the case is closed forever.
notes.oldNote: Affliction shall not rise up the second time (Nahum 1:9). Secured not by force, but by a verdict the whole universe witnessed — which is why this peace is permanent. The case is closed forever. (Same Nahum context note as earlier: Nineveh's local promise is the pattern — when God ends a thing, He ends it so completely it cannot rise again.)
notes.newNote:
Here is where it all lands. Every question that this long war ever raised — about God's fairness, about whether His law was a cage or a kindness — has now been answered in the open, before the whole watching universe. Story of Redemption tells it plainly: the accuser's charges fall silent, and Satan himself bows and confesses that his sentence is just (SR 427). No one is coerced into that verdict; it is simply seen. When the fire has done its work and the earth is made new, one line closes the whole account: "Sin and sinners are no more, God's entire universe is clean, and the great controversy is forever ended" (SR 433).

So this peace isn't held in place by force or by fear of punishment — there is no eternally burning threat kept around to frighten anyone into line. It holds because a tested, proven creation has seen for itself what love is and what rebellion costs, and will never choose that road again (GC 504). That is why the promise can be absolute: "Affliction shall not rise up the second time" (Nahum 1:9) — the same word God once spoke over Nineveh, the local pattern of the universal truth. When God ends a thing, He ends it so completely it cannot rise again. The case is closed. No appeal, no round two — just one pulse of harmony beating through all of it, forever.

notes.beat: Revelation 3:20 — He knocks, He does not break in; the God who refused to win the cosmos by force will not force you either.
notes.oldNote: Revelation 3:20 — He knocks; He does not break in. The God who refused to win the cosmos by force will not force you either. Consistent to the last page. He knocks — and the door only opens from the inside. This is that door, opened; the hand reaching through is the one that would never push it.
notes.newNote:
Rewind to the very first page of this whole story. When Lucifer raised his rebellion, Story of Redemption says God "could at once have hurled this archdeceiver from heaven" — one word, and it was over. He didn't. He refused to settle heaven by raw force, because a loyalty you crush into place isn't loyalty at all. He wanted to be loved because He is worthy of love, never because no one dared say no.

Hold that thread all the way to the last book of the Bible, and it hasn't frayed once. Revelation 3:20: "Behold, I stand at the door, and knock." Not a battering ram — a knock. And notice where the handle is: this door has no latch on the outside. It only opens from the inside. The One who wouldn't force the cosmos will not force you.

Ellen White says every kindness, every warning, every ache of conscience that ever turned you toward Him — that was Him, knocking. Driven back by a stubborn heart, she writes, He doesn't quit; He "returns to plead with greater force" — and the only force He uses is the winning power of His love.

(Let the image sit — the door standing open, the hand reaching through. That's the hand that would never push. It's just waiting for yours.)

notes.beat: The Night 1 five-criteria wager callback lands on the fifth criterion — benevolent; the speaker refuses to stamp the verdict, the room decides.
notes.oldNote: The criteria callback — Night 1's wager finally lands. Recall it gently: 'If a source met all five criteria — consistent record, above human origin, practical, universal, benevolent — would you follow it?' Nights 1 and 2 carried the first four. Tonight was the fifth and hardest: benevolent — does it seek your good, does it fix what is broken? Do NOT stamp the verdict for them: 'I'm not going to check that box for you. You've seen the character of God tonight — the freedom, the cross, the promise. You judge.' Then the ask.
notes.newNote:
Back on the first night I asked you to make a wager. If a source met all five criteria — a consistent record, something above mere human origin, practical, universal, and benevolent — would you follow it? Nights 1 and 2 quietly carried the first four across the line. Tonight was the fifth, and the hardest one to fake: benevolent. Does it actually seek your good? Does it move to fix what's broken in you and in the world?

Here is the discipline of the moment — do NOT stamp the verdict for them. Hand the pen back: "I'm not going to check that box for you. You've watched the character of God all night — the freedom He risks giving, the cross He was willing to bear, the promise of a world made whole. That one's yours to judge." Let it sit a beat. Then the ask.

notes.beat: The ask, both lanes: study with me, or start alone in John; the story has chapters still ahead in Daniel and Revelation.
notes.oldNote: The ask, both lanes: study with me (one hour, any week night), or start alone in the Gospel of John. 'O taste and see that the LORD is good' (Psalm 34:8). You've met His character tonight — the next move is yours. One more pull: everything after the cross tonight — the return, the judgment, the world made new — came from Daniel and Revelation. That is exactly where the studies go next; the story you just heard has chapters still ahead. Close warm; prayer if the room allows.
notes.newNote:
Here's the ask, and there are two ways in. Come study with me — one hour, any week night, no pressure. Or if that's too much too soon, start alone tonight: open the Gospel of John and read. That's it. The Psalmist says, "O taste and see that the LORD is good" — don't take my word for it, prove it for yourself. You've met His character tonight; you've seen how He carries suffering, how He refuses to force a single heart. The next move is yours.

And one more pull before you go. Everything I put in front of you after the cross tonight — His return, the judgment, the whole world made new — I didn't invent any of it. It came straight out of Daniel and Revelation. That's exactly where these studies go next. The story you just heard has chapters still ahead — and there's a seat for you when we open them.

(Close warm. If the room allows, pray.)
